query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐entropy alloy multilayer protective coatings, sharp, engineered chemical gradients at the interfaces induce pronounced local lattice distortions and chemical ordering that raise the effective activation energies for both dislocation climb and atomic diffusion, thereby slowing time‐dependent plastic deformation compared to homogeneous HEA coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: A high‐entropy alloy (HEA) protective coating with a nominal, homogenized composition and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Fabricate multilayer coatings by sequentially depositing two (or more) distinct HEA compositions that differ in key constituent elements to produce sharp compositional gradients at the layer interfaces; in one set the gradients are maintained, while in a controlled comparison set a post‐deposition annealing treatment homogenizes the interface chemistry.
generation.conditions: Creep testing under elevated temperature and stress regimes typical of protective coating applications (e.g., intermediate to high temperatures where both dislocation-mediated and diffusion-mediated mechanisms are active).
generation.structural_mediator: Engineered, chemically heterogeneous interfaces that produce local lattice misfit and ordering, which serve as robust barriers to dislocation motion and suppress rapid atomistic diffusion.
generation.mechanism: The chemically sharp interfaces create localized lattice distortions and regions of enhanced bonding heterogeneity. These features increase the activation energy required for dislocation climb and impede grain-boundary or interfacial diffusion, resulting in a reduction of the steady-state creep rate.
generation.predicted_outcome: Multilayer coatings with maintained sharp interfacial chemical gradients will exhibit lower creep strain rates (or extended creep life) compared with both homogeneous HEA coatings and multilayers in which the interfaces have been homogenized through annealing.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous HEA protective coatings with no deliberate interfacial chemical gradients.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective when individual layer thicknesses are above a critical limit (to support distinct lattice regions) and at temperatures where time-dependent plastic deformation is governed by dislocation climb and diffusion (i.e., intermediate-to-high temperature regimes). Extreme nanolayering or creep regimes dominated by other failure modes may not follow this behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While molecular dynamics studies on dual-phase HEAs (e.g., PMC12842692::web::031::4_conclusions) and nanoindentation studies (e.g., PMC7516662::web::016::5_conclusions) support roles for interfacial dislocation pinning and diffusion‐controlled processes, transferring these mechanisms to a deliberately engineered multilayer architecture introduces uncertainties in optimum layer thickness, composition differences, and the magnitude of the interfacial lattice distortions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multilayer HEA coatings with identical overall thickness and layer architecture. One set is fabricated with intentional, sharp chemical gradients at the interfaces (using controlled deposition parameters) and is left as-deposited; the other set is subjected to a homogenization anneal to blur the interfacial gradients. Subject both sets to identical creep experiments at a fixed elevated temperature and applied stress. Measure the steady-state creep rate and rupture life.
measurements: Creep strain vs. time curves under controlled thermal and stress conditions
Microstructural characterization (e.g., TEM/EDS) to confirm interfacial chemical gradients or homogenization
Measurement of activation energies (e.g., via strain rate sensitivity analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered multilayer coatings (with sharp chemical gradients) do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in steady-state creep rate or an increase in creep life relative to both the homogeneous HEA coatings and the homogenized multilayers, then the hypothesis that chemically induced interfacial lattice distortions are responsible for enhanced creep resistance is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The preceding analyses clearly indicate that under identical creep conditions, the HESA exhibits a significantly lower creep rate than the HEA, thereby demonstrating superior creep resistance. This section elucidates the underlying reasons for this difference from the perspective of microstructural evolution. Figure 10 presents the creep deformation behavior of HESA under extreme conditions (1000 K and 2.5 GPa), with distinct phase identification via color coding: the γ matrix phase is shown in purple, and the γ′ precipitates are depicted in green. The microstructural evolution reveals continuous dislocation generation at GBs, followed by their subsequent propagation into grain interiors. As creep time progresses, additional slip systems become activated, leading to concurrent dislocation motion within the same grain. This results in the formation of parallel slip bands, which are clearly observed in Figure 10. One of the key features observed is the pronounced hindering effect of the γ/γ′ interface on dislocation motion. A clear transition in creep mechanisms is observed, evolving from diffusion-dominated deformation at low stresses to dislocation nucleation, glide, and interaction at intermediate conditions, and ultimately to stress-induced phase transformation at higher stresses and temperatures. This progression is corroborated by atomic-scale structural evolution and steady-state creep theory. Under identical conditions, HESAs show markedly superior creep resistance to HEAs, mainly due to the strong blocking effect of γ/γ′ interfaces on dislocation motion and atomic transport. Both the γ/γ′ lattice misfit and γ′ volume fraction exert a critical influence on creep resistance. The relationship between misfit magnitude and creep behavior is non-monotonic: moderate negative misfit enhances interfacial coherency and stabilizes the microstructure, thereby improving creep resistance, whereas excessively large misfit increases interfacial strain energy and deteriorates performance. A negative misfit is generally more effective in resisting creep because it strengthens the γ/γ′ interface and reduces dislocation transmissibility. In summary, indentation creep tests for reduced activity HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr HEAs were performed by static and dynamic loads at 298 K, 423 K and 573 K. The creep mechanism of the alloys were compared in terms of stress exponent and activation volume. Comparison of the creep resistance of the three systems was done based on creep displacement and activation energy. The following conclusions were drawn: The creep exponent was in the range of 20–140 and activation volume was in the range of 13–20b3, indicating that the time-dependent deformations for all alloys were dislocation dominated. The stress exponent decreased with increasing temperature owing to thermally activated dislocations and the reduction was sharper for HEAs compared to pure W. The creep exponent increased with increasing load (depth) leading to an apparent size effect due to a higher generation rate of dislocation and their entanglement at larger penetration depth. A higher diffusion/annihilation rate of dislocations near the free surface at a smaller depth may be another possible explanation.
